newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Pacific subsea telecoms cable network opened.
newsitem.headline: Asia Pacific subsea telecoms cable network opened.

text.p: Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) on Friday officially opened the last part of the largest single optical fibre cable network in the Asia Pacific region to date.
SingTel said in a statement the Asia Pacific Cable Network (APCN) had been commissioned by 51 telecommunications companies at a total cost of US$640 million.

Planning of the 12,000-km (7,500-mile) network started in 1994 and the network, which has a capacity of five gigabits per second through each of its twin cables, began carrying live traffic in January.

Inaugurating APCN, SingTel's president and chief executive officer Lee Hsien Yang said the network would increase the telecommunications capacity in the Asia Pacific by an additional 800,000 simultaneous telephone channels.
This would be sufficient to meet the needs of the region until the end of the century, he said.

"The APCN, with its large bandwidth and high quality transmission, will provide the high speed backbone for Internet access and other multimedia services such as dial-up video and interactive TV," Lee said.

SingTel officials said APCN complemented the giant SEA-ME-WE 3 submarine cable network which is due to be completed by 1999 and will run from Asia and Australia, across the Middle East and Africa to Western Europe.
Awards worth more than US$300 million for the third and final stage of the 39,000-km (23,600-mile) SEA-ME-WE 3 cable network would be made this month, officials told Reuters earlier on Friday.
The SEA-ME-WE 3 will eventually have around four times the capacity of the APCN, officials say.
The APCN network links Korea, Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan, the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia.
It also provides a direct optical link between Australia and the rest of Asia.
Lee told reporters the cable would help contribute to the gradual lowering of telephone call charges across Asia.
"This cable certainly lowers our cost and we expect the trend of lower costs to continue," he said.
He declined to say if SingTel would cut its charges as a result of the greater cable capacity, saying the company's charges were based on commercial considerations.
"If we are able to improve those costs...we will see if the competitive position is such that we want to reduce our prices," he said.
He said the APCN offered the region diversity and protection from disruption of telecommunications services because it had three separate systems.
"To have more cables means the customer has more peace of mind," he told reporters. "Even if a trawler...cuts one cable, we will be able to restore the line."
